opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic reason is that if you just pick projects that seem locally interesting or locally useful, it's pretty easy to end up working on things that don't actually matter much for the outcome. There are a lot of research directions that sound safety-relevant but, when you think about how things will actually go, aren't the bottleneck, or would happen anyway, or only help in worlds where we were going to be fine regardless.

So what we try to do is sketch out, concretely: what does the situation look like when we have very powerful AI systems? What are the companies plausibly going to do, given realistic levels of political will and caution? What are the main threat models, like AIs that are scheming against us, or that sabotage safety work? And then what would a reasonable plan for handling that look like? What measures would a developer need, and in what order?

Once you have even a rough version of that, a lot falls out. You can see which pieces are missing, which ones nobody is working on, and which ones are on the critical path. Control is a good example. When we thought about the plan, it seemed like in a lot of realistic worlds we won't be confident our models are aligned, and we'll still want to use them for a bunch of useful work, including safety research. So you need some way to get useful work out of models that might be trying to undermine you. That suggested a whole research agenda that wasn't really being pursued, and it came pretty directly from thinking about the overall plan rather than from looking for a cool project.

It also helps with prioritization within a project. If you know what role the work is supposed to play, you know what level of rigor matters, what assumptions are reasonable, and when something is good enough to move on.

I'd add the caveat that these plans are very rough and will definitely be wrong in many ways. The point isn't to have a perfect blueprint. It's more that having an explicit picture, even a flawed one, forces you to confront the question "how does this actually help?" and lets you notice when your work is disconnected from that. I think the field as a whole would benefit from more of this kind of end-to-end thinking, and from people writing down their plans so others can critique them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses realistic political will and which measures a developer might need, but it does not pose the specific scenario of a responsible AI company having a three-month lead with very low political will.

r002.rationale: It says that thinking through the overall plan suggested a research agenda around control that was not otherwise being pursued, linking AI control research to Redwood’s planning work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic reason is that if you don't have an overall picture of what you're trying to accomplish, it's really hard to tell whether any individual project is actually load-bearing. There's a huge number of things you could work on in AI safety that are locally interesting, where you can make progress and write a paper, but then when you step back and ask "okay, how does this fit into the world actually going well?" the answer is kind of unclear.

So the way I think about it is: you want to start from something like a story of how things might go. What's the situation going to look like when we have AIs that are roughly as capable as humans at AI research, or somewhat more capable? What are the main ways that could go badly? What's the realistic set of things that AI developers would actually be willing to do in that situation, given commercial pressure and limited time? And then, given all of that, what's the plan that gets you to a reasonable outcome?

Once you have something like that written down, even if it's rough and you expect a lot of it to be wrong, it becomes much easier to do project selection. You can look at a candidate project and ask, "which part of the plan does this help with? If this succeeded, what would change about what we'd do or what we'd recommend to a lab?" And often you find that a project you were excited about doesn't actually connect to anything, or it connects to a part of the plan that's already in decent shape, and there's some other part that's totally neglected where the marginal work is way more valuable.

The control agenda is kind of an example of this. We didn't start by saying "let's do red-teaming experiments on code backdoors." We started by asking: suppose alignment research doesn't fully pan out, and we have AIs that might be scheming against us. What could a developer realistically do in that situation? And then the control framing — ensure safety even if the models are misaligned — falls out of that, and then the specific experiments are things you'd want to run to figure out whether the framing actually works.

There's also just a coordination benefit. If you have a bunch of researchers and everyone's running their own thing, you end up with a portfolio that's basically a random sample of what people found interesting. If there's a shared plan, people can argue about the plan, and that disagreement is often much more productive than disagreement about individual projects, because it's where the real cruxes are.

I'd add the caveat that you don't want to be too rigid about it. The plan is going to be wrong in a bunch of ways, and some of the best work comes from someone noticing something that the plan didn't anticipate. But I think the failure mode of "no overall plan, lots of locally reasonable projects" is a lot more common in the field than the failure mode of "too committed to a plan," so on the margin I think more planning is good.

r001.rationale: The response does not raise the question of prioritizing alignment measures under a three-month lead and very low political will.

r002.rationale: It presents the control agenda as an example of planning from an overall account of how things could go, and says the control framing follows from that analysis.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s pretty easy to come up with a project that seems relevant to AI safety, but much harder to explain how that project actually leads to the world going better. So we want to start with something like: suppose we succeeded at this research. Who would use the results? What would they do differently? And would that be enough to substantially reduce the risk, or are there other problems that would prevent the plan from working?

Writing down an overall plan forces you to confront those questions. You might discover that the project you were excited about is addressing something that isn’t really a bottleneck, or that it depends on another problem being solved that you don’t have a good approach to.

And then individual projects can be attempts to resolve particular uncertainties in that plan. The plan doesn’t have to be right, and you should expect to revise it. But having it makes it much easier to tell whether you’re making useful progress, as opposed to just producing results that sound safety-relevant.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses evaluating projects and bottlenecks, but does not pose the specific scenario of a responsible AI company having a three-month lead and very low political will, or ask which alignment measures to prioritize.

r002.rationale: It says overall plans help assess whether projects make useful progress, but does not tentatively attribute the emergence of AI control research to Redwood’s planning work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s easy to work on something that seems useful in isolation without having a good story for how it leads to things going well overall. You might have an interesting research question, and you can make progress on it, but even if you succeed, it might not address a bottleneck that actually matters.

So we try to start with something like: suppose AI develops in a particular way. What would we need to do to avoid catastrophe? Which parts of that could plausibly be handled by other people, and where are there important gaps? Then we can work backwards to projects that would help fill those gaps.

That doesn’t mean we expect the plan to be right in detail. A lot of the point is to make our assumptions explicit, so we can notice when they’re wrong. And a project can be valuable partly because it helps us figure out whether the overall plan is viable. But having the plan gives us a way to distinguish between making progress on an interesting problem and making progress towards the outcome we actually care about.
